I. 
BY THE COMMISSION 
A. 
Statement 
1. 
Through this Decision we grant, with clarifications, the Application for Rehearing, 
Reargument, or Reconsideration (“RRR”) of Decision No. C25-0892 that Trial Staff of the 
Public Utilities Commission (“Staff”), the Colorado Energy Office (“CEO”), and the Colorado 
Office of the Utility Consumer Advocate (“UCA”) (collectively, the “State Agencies”) filed on 
December 30, 2025. We also grant in part, with clarifications, and deny, in part, the RRR that 
Public Service Company of Colorado (“Public Service” or the “Company”) filed on 
December 30, 2025. Finally, we deny the RRR that CORE Electric Cooperative (“CORE”) filed 
on December 30, 2025. 
2. 
Through this Decision the Commission also grants the Motions for Leave to 
Respond filed on January 12, 2026, by Western Resource Advocates (“WRA”), the Environmental 
Justic Coalition (“EJC”), and the Conservation Coalition, respectively. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
3 
B. 
Background 
3. 
On November 10, 2025, Staff, CEO, UCA, and Public Service (the “Joint 
Petitioners”) filed a Joint Petition seeking a variance from Ordering Paragraphs 1 and 2 of Decision 
No. C18-0761,1 and any other decisions the Commission deems necessary, to modify the planned 
retirement date of Comanche Unit 2 (“Pueblo Unit 2”) from December 31, 2025, to 
December 31, 2026 (“Joint Petition”). 
4. 
In Decision No. C25-0892,2 the Commission granted, with modifications, the Joint 
Petition. In extending the life of Pueblo Unit 2, the Commission rejected requests from certain 
parties for a hearing, discovery, and answer testimony. The Commission reasoned that such due 
process will be afforded subsequently—particularly in the Step 2 application filing and when 
Public Service seeks to recover the costs associated with Unit 3’s outage—but that the Commission 
must move swiftly to allow Unit 2 to continue operating.3 As part of its decision to extend the life 
of Pueblo Unit 2, the Commission found that Unit 3’s prolonged, unplanned outage is the single 
justification for extending Unit 2.4 The Commission also stressed that there is no presumption of 
prudence for the repair of Unit 3 or operation of Unit 2. The Commission stated that 
“Public Service cannot assume that repairing Unit 3 is a prudent approach if better alternatives are 
available.”5 
5. 
In connection with Unit 2’s extension, the Commission directed additional 
reporting and future filings. To begin, the Commission largely adopted the two-step process put 
forth in the Joint Petition, consisting of the March 1, 2026 report and analysis (Step 1) and the 

1 Issued September 10, 2018, in Proceeding No. 16A-0396E. 
2 Issued December 10, 2025. 
3 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 64. 
4 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 65. 
5 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 70. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
4 
application filing the Company must file no later than June 1, 2026 (Step 2).6 The Commission 
went further than what the Joint Petitioners proposed, however, and required monthly reports 
containing additional information. One of the reporting requirements was for the Company to 
report any estimated material future capital costs for the repair of Unit 3 before such costs are 
obligated.7 
6. 
In addition to the reporting, the Commission placed operational limitations on 
Unit 2 and Unit 3 so that the two units together could not generate more than 3,942,000 MWh in 
2026. This 3,942,000 MWh limit is what Unit 3 could produce in 2026 given its 60 percent annual 
capacity factor limit agreed upon in the 2021 ERP.8 The Commission reasoned: “Given that 
Unit 2 and Unit 3 are now intended to work together to do the work that Unit 3 would have done 
but for its closure, it is reasonable to apply Unit 3’s operational limit from the 2021 ERP to both 
units.”9 The Commission noted that Public Service could file an appropriate request supported by 
testimony and other evidence if the Company had concerns with the 3,942,000 MWh limitation.10 
7. 
Chair Blank dissented from the operational limitations, opining that he would only 
require additional reporting on the collective operation of Unit 2 and Unit 3. Chair Blank expressed 
concerns about non-economic dispatch and how much the operational limitation would cost.11 
8. 
As referenced above, on December 30, 2025, the State Agencies, Public Service, 
and CORE each filed RRRs regarding Decision No. C25-0892. 

6 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 69. 
7 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 73. 
8 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 77. 
9 Decision No. C25-0892 at ¶ 78.

9. 
On January 12, 2026, WRA, EJC, and Conservation Coalition each filed a Motion 
for Leave to Respond to the Company’s RRR. 
10. 
Public Service filed a Response in Opposition on January 20, 2026. 
C. 
Motions for Leave to Respond 
11. 
WRA, EJC, and Conservation Coalition each filed a Motion for Leave to Respond 
pursuant to Rule 1506(b), 4 Code of Colorado Regulations 723-1. Rule 1506(b) states that no 
response to an application for RRR may be filed expect upon motion and that any such motion 
must demonstrate one of the following: a material misrepresentation of a fact in the record; an 
incorrect statement or error of law; an attempt to introduce facts not in evidence; accident or 
surprise, which ordinary prudence could not have guarded against; or newly discovered facts or 
issues material for the moving party which that party could not, with reasonable diligence, have 
discovered prior to the time the application for RRR was filed. 
12. 
WRA seeks leave to respond because it contends Public Service’s RRR contains 
material misrepresentations of the Commission’s decision and incorrect statements of law 
regarding the operational limit for Pueblo Units 2 and 3. Specifically, WRA argues the Company 
mischaracterizes the limit as a “hard cap” requiring pre-approval, contrary to the Commission’s 
intent and the Updated Settlement Agreement (“USA”) in the Company’s 2021 Electric Resource 
Plan/Clean Energy Plan (“ERP/CEP”). 
13. 
EJC argues Public Service’s RRR include incorrect statements of law, material 
misrepresentations of fact, and new facts not in the Petition. EJC contends, for example, that the 
Company downplays emissions benefits, mischaracterizes the Commission’s decision, and 
introduces new proposals and information such as eliminating the 60% capacity factor limit for 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
6 
Unit 3 and reporting requirements for repair costs. EJC asserts these circumstances satisfy 
Rule 1506(b)’s criteria for granting leave to respond. 
14. 
Conservation Coalition alleges Public Service’s filing misrepresents the 
Commission’s decision, introduces facts not in evidence, and raises new arguments not contained 
in the Joint Petition. Conservation Coalition asserts the Company incorrectly claims the 
Commission invented a new operational limit, misstate settlement provisions, and for the first time 
requests removal of Unit 3’s generation cap. Conservation Coalition states these 
misrepresentations and surprises justify granting leave to respond. 
15. 
In the Company’s Response in Opposition, it contends none of the motions meet 
the standard under Rule 1506(b), and argues its RRR filing does not introduce new evidence or 
create unfair surprise, as the differences between Pueblo Units 2 and 3 and the absence of 
operational restrictions on Unit 2 in the USA are well-established facts of which the Commission 
can take administrative notice. Public Service further states its legal arguments regarding 
operational limits were foreseeable and that the issues raised in the motions can be addressed in 
the forthcoming June 1 application. Accordingly, Public Service requests that the Commission 
deny the motions for leave to respond 
16. 
We find good cause to grant the respective motions for leave to respond pursuant 
to Rule 1506(b). In this Proceeding, the motions reasonably assert that certain facts and 
issues—such as the estimated costs for Unit 3 repairs as well as expenditures already 
incurred—were raised for the first time in the Company’s RRR filings. Additionally, because this 
is an expedited Proceeding with limited opportunities for party input, granting these motions in 
this instance will allow for more fulsome participation in a fast-moving process. For these reasons, 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
7 
the Commission finds it appropriate to exercise its discretion and grant the motions for leave to 
respond. 
D. 
Operational Limitations 
1. 
RRR Arguments 
17. 
In their Joint RRR, the State Agencies request the Commission remove the 
operational restriction on Unit 2 and Unit 3. They warn that unintended consequences of the 
operational limitation could result in significant costs being imposed on ratepayers through 
non-economic dispatch and the operational challenges of applying Unit 3’s capacity factor limit to 
the combination of Units 2 and 3 over different operational time periods. The State Agencies argue 
the Commission should defer to Public Service to implement the Unit 2 extension in line with its 
standard operating and dispatch procedures. The State Agencies express agreement with Chair 
Blank’s dissent from the operational limitation and his expressed concerns about non-economic 
dispatch and how much the operational limitation would cost.12 
18. 
The State Agencies note the Commission traditionally does not specifically direct 
the utility’s engineering practices, and the Commission should follow that practice here. 
They assert the operational restriction limits the Company’s ability to decide what is prudent and 
necessary in light of maintenance, safety and reliability concerns, and interferes with engineering 
and management practices that should be left to the Company. The State Agencies recommend 
that the Commission “squarely place the burden of prudent operations on the Company, including 
by granting it full control of unit operations.”13 

12 Joint RRR at p. 1. 
13 Joint RRR at p. 3. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
8 
19. 
Moreover, the State Agencies express skepticism of the practical impact the 
operational limitations will have on reducing emissions. They argue that because Unit 2 is less 
than half the capacity of Unit 3, and Unit 3 is not expected to return to service before June 2026, 
it is unlikely that the combined operations would have a significant impact on emissions. 
In addition, the State Agencies note that if the constraint is hit, any resources the Company acquires 
on the market may be associated with increased emissions. 14 The State Agencies conclude that the 
continued operation of Unit 2 in 2026, without operational limitations, is the most cost-effective 
approach to providing needed electricity for the system. 
20. 
Public Service also challenges the operational limitations on Unit 2 and Unit 3. 
First, the Company argues the Decision’s operational limitations actually “inverts the settled, and 
previously Commission-approved, arrangement” for capacity factor limits for Unit 3 in the USA.15 
Public Service acknowledges that in the USA the Company agreed to operate Unit 3 at a maximum 
annual capacity factor of 60 percent for 2026. The Company argues, however, that this capacity 
factor limit was not an absolute bar on operating the unit if needed for reliability purposes. 
As support, the Company quotes paragraph 38 below from the USA: 
In the case of an extraordinary event(s) that the Company exceeds the 
maximum annual capacity factor for a given year, the Company will make 
a filing in its Electric Commodity Adjustment (“ECA”) annual prudence 
review to explain the circumstances that led to the need to exceed the 
maximum annual capacity factor.16 
21. 
Instead of the after-the-fact ECA review process agreed upon in the USA, 
Public Service argues the Commission appears to impose a hard cap on energy production from 

14 Joint RRR at p. 4. 
15 Public Service RRR at p. 11. 
16 Public Service RRR at p. 12 (quoting USA at ¶ 38). 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
9 
which the Company cannot deviate without advance Commission approval. Public Service argues 
these changes to the USA are not workable or practical. 
22. 
The Company further argues the capacity limits agreed upon in the USA are subject 
to paragraph 41 of the USA that provides that “[p]rocuring adequate flexible, dispatchable 
generation is imperative to allow for the early reduced operations set forth in this proposal and a 
reliable system.”17 Public Service argues it has faced challenges in procuring dispatchable 
generation at the same time it has seen demand growth. 
23. 
In addition to its arguments relating to the USA, Public Service argues the 
operational limitations could be costly, have unintended consequences, and may not ultimately 
reduce emissions. The Company asserts that Chair Blank’s dissent is correct in that operating to a 
hard cap for Units 2 and 3 will result in non-economic dispatch if the operational limitation is 
binding. Public Service asserts the resulting additional costs could “easily range into the millions 
or even tens of millions of dollars….”18 Despite these additional costs, the Company warns the 
operational limitation may simply cause less efficient units more frequently. 
24. 
As for the unintended consequences, Public Service notes that Unit 2, which was 
built in the 1970s and nearing the end of its life, is much older than Unit 3. The Company asserts 
that both Unit 2 and Unit 3 are designed to run at stable power levels for long periods of time, and 
more frequent cycling can lead to malfunctions or damage—particularly with Unit 2.19 
The Company warns the operational limitation could jeopardize the Commission’s suggested 
option of running Unit 2 through 2030. 

17 Public Service RRR at p. 14 (quoting USA at ¶ 41). 
18 Public Service RRR at p. 13. 
19 Public Service RRR at p. 13. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
10 
25. 
Finally, Public Service argues in the alternative that if the Commission retains the 
operational limitation for Unit 2 and Unit 3, the Commission should at least follow the process set 
forth in the USA. Specifically, the Company requests the Commission eliminate the requirement 
that Public Service seek pre-approval to exceed the operational limitation and instead adopt the 
after-the-fact ECA review process in paragraph 38 of the USA. Public Service argues the USA’s 
ECA review process allows the Company to make operational decisions in real-time without 
day-to-day Commission oversight.20 
2. 
Responses to the RRRs 
26. 
In its Response, EJC argues the State Agencies and Public Service materially 
misrepresent the facts regarding the emissions benefits of the operational restrictions. EJC notes 
that coal-fired power plants typically emit greater amounts of air pollution and greenhouse gases 
than other types of generation resources. EJC therefore states that it is “quite doubtful” that 
electricity from other sources would have higher emissions.21 EJC further argues the other sources 
of electricity would not harm community members in Pueblo to the same extent: “the air pollution 
emitted by generation resources is not fungible, and the location, the amount, and the types of 
pollution emitted by generation facilities matter greatly to impacted communities.”22 In addition, 
EJC argues removing the operational constraint would be directly contrary to Senate Bill 21-272’s 
equity mandate. 
27. 
EJC also contests the State Agencies’ claim that the operational limit introduces 
complex and unplanned capacity factor limits. EJC argues the requirement that Public Service not 
generate more than 3.942 million MWh at the Pueblo coal plant in 2026 is not complex because it 

20 Public Service RRR at p. 14. 
21 EJC RRR Response at p. 4. 
22 EJC RRR Response at p. 5. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
11 
provide Public Service significant discretion on how to operate the two units. EJC asserts it is not 
unplanned because the limit is derived from the USA. 
28. 
EJC asserts Public Service and the State Agencies, for the first time in RRR, seek 
to remove the 60 percent capacity limit on Unit 3. EJC notes the Joint Petition does not ask the 
Commission to eliminate or modify the 60 percent capacity factor limit for Unit 3 in 2026. In RRR, 
however, these parties now request the Commission allow Public Service to dispatch both units at 
its discretion, effectively eliminating the 60 percent capacity factor limit. EJC asserts this 
constitutes a “surprise” to EJC justifying EJC’s RRR Response.23 
29. 
Conservation Coalition argues the Commission should uphold the operational 
limitations on Unit 2 and Unit 3. As support, Conservation Coalition claims the Company now has 
additional capacity that was not available when the Joint Petition was filed. To be clear, 
Conservation Coalition does not request the Commission reject the extension of Unit 2 in light of 
this new capacity. Rather, they argue the new capacity further supports the operational 
limitations.24 
30. 
Conservation Coalition also argues Public Service’s statements in RRR undermine 
the assertion that in the absence of a generation limit, Units 2 and 3 would be dispatched 
economically. Conservation Coalition states “the Company claims that coal units like Comanche 
2 and 3 are inherently incapable of cycling. ‘Both units are designed to run at stable power levels 
for long periods of time, and more frequent cycling can lead to malfunctions or, potentially, 
damage.’”25 Conservation Coalition asserts that if Unit 3 mut run at stable power levels for long 
periods of time, that would impact the extent to which they can be economically dispatched in any 

23 EJC RRR Response at p. 10. 
24 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 6. 
25 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 6 (quoting Public Service RRR at p. 13). 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
12 
meaningful sense of that term. Conservation Coalition concludes that the Commission cannot grant 
RRR based on arguments that are in tension with the Company’s own statements in its RRR and 
previously in Proceeding No. 21A-0141E. Conservation Coalition argues the Joint Petitioners 
misrepresent the Commission’s decision when they assert the operational limitations substitute the 
Commission preference for the Company’s engineering judgment. Conservation Coalition argues 
the Company—not the Commission—first proposed the operational limitation on Unit 3 via the 
USA. 
31. 
Conservation Coalition adds that it does not oppose the Commission clarifying that 
paragraph 38 of the USA (allowing the Company to exceed the capacity factor restrictions for 
extraordinary events) remains in force and applies to the Commission’s decision extending the 
annual limit to the combined generation from Units 2 and 3.26 Conservation Coalition also states 
the Commission’s operational limitations do not prescribe how the Company operates Units 2 and 
3 to comply with the limit. Rather, deciding which of the units to operate and when is left to the 
discretion of the Company, so long as the annual limit is observed. Conservation Coalition goes 
on to argue the operational limit is not “complex” because Public Service already imposed capacity 
factor limits on Unit 3 for 2025. Arguments that extending the limit to both Unit 3 and Unit 2 
introduces insurmountable complexity are meritless given Unit 3 will be out of service until 
June 2026. 27 
32. 
As for the arguments from the Joint Petitioners that the operational limit would 
provide no emissions benefit, Conservation Coalition asserts this is factually unsupported and 
inconsistent with prior, sworn testimony. Conservation Coalition cites prior testimony from CEO 

26 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 8. 
27 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 9. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
13 
and Public Service in Proceeding No. 21A-0141E urging the Commission to approve those limits 
because of the significant emission reductions they would achieve. Conservation Coalition goes 
on to criticize the suggestions that alternative sources of electricity would be more polluting that 
Unit 2 and Unit 3. In fact, Conservation Coalition argues the Joint Petitioners request to remove 
the operational limitation, even as to Unit 3, could “dramatically increase emissions.”28 
33. 
Conservation Coalition also argues there is no evidence that the annual limit on 
Unit 3 cannot be applied to Unit 2 and that this proposition conflicts with the Company’s 
statements that both Unit 2 and Unit 3 were designed to run at stable power levels for long periods 
of time. 
34. 
More fundamentally, Conservation Coalition argues the annual operational limit 
ensures that once Unit 3 returns to service, there is some constraint on the amount that Unit 2 in 
conjunction with Unit 3. They assert: 
The Company should not be allowed to use the unexpected outage at 
Comanche 3 to achieve what appears to be its true objective here: not to use 
Comanche 2 as a temporary replacement for Comanche 3 while Unit 3 is 
out of service, but to operate Unit 2 with no constraints whatsoever even 
after Unit 3 is back online.29 
35. 
Conservation Coalition maintains that this result would be inconsistent with the 
Commission’s rationale for extending Unit 2. Accordingly, the Commission should uphold the 
operational limitation. 
36. 
Similar to EJC, Conservation Coalition argues that, for the first time in RRR, the 
Joint Petitioners ask the Commission to not apply the operational limitation to Unit 3. Conservation 
Coalition asserts this constitutes a procedurally improper request to revise the Phase I Decision 

28 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 12. 
29 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 14. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
14 
from the 2021 ERP/CEP approving the USA. Conservation Coalition further asserts that while the 
Company seeks to change certain aspects of the USA, it expects the Commission to implement the 
other aspects that financially benefit the Company. Conservation Coalition argues there is “no 
justification for the Company’s invitation for the Commission to cherry-pick which Settlement 
provisions are reexamined and which are not.”30 
37. 
Conservation Coalition also opposes Public Service’s suggestion the capacity 
factor limitation on Unit 3 is contingent on the Company procuring some specific amount of firm, 
dispatchable capacity. Conservation Coalition asserts the capacity factor restrictions in the USA 
are not contingent on any external event such as the Commission approving a specific amount of 
new, dispatchable generation. Moreover, the USA does not provide a numeric target for new 
dispatchable generation, nor does it give the Company authority to deviate from the Settlement if 
the Company believes the Commission has approved less new dispatchable generation than the 
Company prefers.31 
38. 
Finally, Conservation Coalition responds to Public Service’s critique that 
Conservation Coalition and the other parties proposing the operational limitations failed to 
mention paragraph 38 of the USA authorizing the Company to exceed the capacity factor limit in 
extraordinary circumstances. Conservation Coalition asserts “there was no reason for us to mention 
paragraph 38 of the Settlement Agreement because we did not propose any modifications to that 
provision.”32 They add that the USA’s provision authorizing the Company to exceed the capacity 
limit if the Company can justify that exceedance in an ECA filing does not justify eliminating the 
capacity limit altogether. 

30 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 16. 
31 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 16. 
32 Conservation Coalition RRR Response at p. 17. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
15 
39. 
WRA similarly requests the Commission maintain the operational limit as it 
applies to Unit 2 and Unit 3 and clarify that the ECA review process adopted in the USA continues 
to apply. WRA reasons the ECA review approach “is consistent with the Commission’s statement 
that the burden will be on Public Service to demonstrate that exceeding the limit is in the public 
interest.”33 WRA adds that nothing in the Commission’s Decision requires a firm limit from which 
the Company must obtain preapproval to exceed. WRA thus concludes that arguments about the 
operational limitation being a “hard cap” constitute material misrepresentations of the Decision. 
WRA argues a correct interpretation of the Decision is that the Commission invited Public Service 
to modify the operational limitation through an application filed now. 
40. 
WRA argues that under this correct interpretation of the Commission’s Decision, 
maintaining the operational limitation “does not threaten the utility’s ability to make operational 
decisions in real time, does not substitute the Commission’s judgement for the utility’s, and will 
not result in non-economic dispatch.”34 WRA notes the Company’s alternative RRR argument that 
the Commission should at a minimum follow the ECA review process in the USA. From this, 
WRA asserts the Company is comfortable operating its system under such an approach. 
3. 
Findings and Conclusions 
41. 
The Commission grants the RRRs from the State Agencies and Public Service on 
this point, with certain clarifications.35 We are persuaded by the Company’s assertion the 
operational limitations may damage Unit 2, which is much older than Unit 3 and nearing the end 
of its life. The Company’s statements that frequent cycling can lead to malfunctions or damage 

33 WRA RRR Response at p. 4. 
34 WRA RRR Response at p. 5. 
35 Commissioner Plant dissents on this point, in part, in that he would require the Company to apply 
economic dispatch for its generating units including the social cost of carbon. This would ensure cost 
effective dispatch to meet load while ensuring the coal plants are operated as a last resort. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
16 
also indicate the plant is not well-suited for our current system, which is defined by increasing 
amounts of variable generation from renewable resources. When we evaluate the prudency of 
Public Service’s operations of Unit 2 and Unit 3 (presumably in an ECA annual prudency review), 
we intend to examine whether Unit 2’s limitations, including its inability to cycle in the same way 
Unit 3 can, led to uneconomic dispatch of the Company’s system. We also find it appropriate to 
evaluate what would have occurred both in terms of costs and emissions had Unit 3 been available 
to operate as contemplated under the USA. 
42. 
In addition to the Company’s representations regarding Unit 2, we take seriously 
the arguments from the State Agencies that the Commission should allow Public Service to 
implement the Unit 2 extension in line with its standard operating and dispatch procedures and 
that the operational challenges of applying Unit 3’s capacity factor limit to the combination of 
Units 2 and 3 could result in significant costs on ratepayers. In particular, the Commission fully 
agrees with the following: “The State Agencies recommend that the Commission squarely place 
the burden of prudent operations on the Company, including by granting it full control of unit 
operations.”36 
43. 
We acknowledge the operational limitations may not require changes in how the 
Company would run Unit 2, especially prior to when Unit 3 comes back online. 
Ultimately, however, there is insufficient record to confidently predict how Public Service would 
respond to the operational limitations. Public Service may deem it necessary to cycle Unit 2 more 
frequently in the spring of 2026 to ensure that it has sufficient headroom to run Unit 3 as necessary 
during the summer. Arguments from EJC and Conservation Coalition to the contrary are 
unpersuasive. While both coal-fired plants were initially designed to run at stable power levels for 

36 Joint RRR at p. 3. 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
17 
long periods of time, Unit 2 and Unit 3 are not the same. The fact that Public Service agreed in the 
USA to impose capacity factor restrictions on Unit 3 does not mean the Company’s concerns about 
applying those limitations on Unit 2 are unfounded. The burden of prudent operations must remain 
on the Company. 
44. 
The Commission agrees with Conservation Coalition and EJC that the Joint 
Petitioners’ arguments regarding emissions are unpersuasive. It is possible the alternative sources 
of electricity Public Service acquires to replace generation from Unit 3 and Unit 2 could have 
roughly the same emissions. However, the Joint Petitioners put forth no evidence to support this 
claim. It is just as possible the replacement generation could come from cleaner sources of 
electricity, such as renewables or gas. Even assuming the operational restrictions on Unit 2 and 
Unit 3 would reduce emissions during 2026, however, this factor alone does not overcome 
concerns about forcing Public Service to operate Unit 2 in a way that it was not designed to operate. 
45. 
EJC makes a legitimate point that air pollution is not fungible, and the types of 
pollution generating facilities emit matter greatly to the impacted communities. Nevertheless, this 
point does not justify imposing the operational restriction on Unit 2. In addition to the operational 
concerns regarding Unit 2, there is insufficient record to accurately estimate the relative impact of 
removing the operational limit on disproportionately impacted (“DI”) communities. It is possible 
the operational restriction could require the Company to run the Cherokee gas units, which are 
also in a DI community, at a higher capacity factor. While the emissions impact from coal are 
likely worse than the emissions impacts from gas units, such a high level analysis would overlook 
other important factors such as other sources of pollution the communities near the Cherokee units 
already face. While the Commission must consider how its decisions impact DI communities, there 

Before the Public Utilities Commission of the State of Colorado 
Decision No. C26-0067 
PROCEEDING NO. 25V-0480E 
18 
is insufficient record here to assume the operational limitation on Unit 2 will result in a net benefit 
to DI communities across Colorado. 
46.

76. 
In addition, we disagree with the Company’s characterization of the Commission’s 
resource adequacy proceedings. In the 2021 ERP/CEP the Commission’s approved portfolio 
included more thermal resources than the Company’s preferred portfolio, and we rejected 
arguments in RRR to reduce the amount of thermal resources, reasoning that doing so could risk 
reliability. While one of the thermal resources in the approved Phase II portfolio failed, the 
Commission established a backup selection process by which the Company could have established 
Bid 1000 as the replacement.67 Acknowledging the need to be able to quickly shift to backup 
projects, the Commission also invited the Company to file a petition for waiver of the backup bid 
selection process as circumstances require.68 The Company elected not to use these procedures but 
instead waited until its Motion to Approve the CEP Delivery to address Bid 1000. 
77. 
More broadly, the Commission has set up flexible resource acquisition processes 
and has been responsive to stakeholder requests to pursue novel regulatory processes to address 
quickly changing circumstances and rising costs. These include the backup bid selection process, 
the CEP Delivery Plan, the interim just transition solicitation and its Phase II Framework, the 
near-term procurement process, and this current proceeding in which the Commission achieved 
the accelerated timeframe for a written decision one month after the Joint Petition was filed.
